Do LMs Know What Variables Do? Interpreting Code Representations via Variable Roles

Célian Vasson Affiliation: Sorbonne Université    Daniil Ognev Affiliation: MBZUAI    Kentaro Inui Affiliation: MBZUAI Affiliation: RIKEN AIP Affiliation: Tohoku University    Benjamin Heinzerling Affiliation: RIKEN AIP Affiliation: Tohoku University
Abstract

Variable roles describe recurring behaviors such as accumulation, traversal, and retaining the best candidate encountered. We use Sajaniemi’s independently defined taxonomy to study which role distinctions can be recovered from large language models, how sparse autoencoders (SAEs) retain those distinctions, and whether associated directions support control of generation. We introduce static annotation rules for all eleven roles and a corpus of 126,926 natural-code files across five languages. Across five model–SAE systems, residual probes outperform individual SAE features and tested lexical baselines, with modest losses after neutral target renaming. Combining SAE features closes much of the single-feature gap, but probes on SAE reconstructions are less sensitive to role-changing edits reviewed by LLMs. High paired ranking accuracy coexists with frequent false positives at fixed thresholds. During generation, interventions often change role annotations at the cost of correctness; changes accompanied by passing tests show no clear aggregate advantage over random controls. The benchmark separates role-related recoverability, SAE fidelity, and correctness-preserving control through matched prediction, source edits, and generation interventions.

1 Introduction

Large language models generate and modify source code, from code completion to agents that plan, edit, and test software (Jiang et al., 2024; Dong et al., 2025). Yet programming success alone does not establish which program properties a model represents: models may exploit identifiers and familiar code patterns, and their performance can change under controlled input transformations (Hooda et al., 2024). We investigate this question through the behavior of individual variables. A variable may advance through a predictable sequence, accumulate values, or retain the best candidate seen so far. These behaviors depend on relationships across updates: recognizing an addition alone does not distinguish a regular progression from accumulation of input-dependent data. The same behavior can also use different names and language constructs, motivating three questions: which role distinctions are recoverable, how faithfully do sparse autoencoders retain them, and can associated directions change generation while preserving correctness?

We investigate these questions using Sajaniemi’s variable roles, developed in the psychology of programming to characterize recurring uses of variables (Sajaniemi, 2002; Sajaniemi and Navarro Prieto, 2005). The taxonomy defines behavioral criteria independently of the models under study. Prior studies recover program structure and intermediate execution states from model representations (Hernández López et al., 2022; Jin and Rinard, 2024) and find shared representations across programming languages (Kargaran et al., 2025; Yin et al., 2026). We extend these analyses to variable behavior through matched prediction, controlled source edits, and generation interventions.

We combine program analysis with sparse autoencoder (SAE) features and probes, contributing:

  • •

    Large-scale multilingual dataset and benchmark. We introduce a dataset of 126,926 natural-code files across five programming languages, to our knowledge the first to automatically annotate all eleven Sajaniemi variable roles at this scale. We construct a benchmark with matched and mined negatives, LLM-reviewed role-changing edits, and role-preserving target renaming to measure recoverability under controlled comparisons. We will publicly release the benchmark, annotations, evaluation splits, and extraction pipeline, with instructions for reconstructing the corpus.

  • •

    Recoverability and SAE fidelity. Across five model–SAE systems, we compare residual probes, reconstruction probes, individual features, and probes combining 64 features at observation points after the selected operation. Controlled edits test sensitivity beyond matched prediction; language, implementation, and readout comparisons qualify recoverability.

  • •

    Limits of intervention-based control. We measure role induction and suppression alongside functional correctness and random-direction controls. Annotation changes are substantially more frequent than changes accompanied by passing tests; Figure 1 illustrates a selected successful repair.

2 Background: Variable Roles in Program Comprehension

Program comprehension and programming knowledge.

Research on human program comprehension distinguishes representations of operations and control flow from a situation model of program goals, with task-dependent prominence (Pennington, 1987). Programming plans describe familiar patterns of operations that accomplish particular goals (Soloway and Ehrlich, 1984). Sajaniemi’s roles bring this perspective to individual variables through variable plans, or stereotyped uses of variables. The taxonomy originated in textbook programs; subsequent card sorting and interviews with professional programmers recovered groupings consistent with the roles, alongside variation in behavioral interpretations (Sajaniemi and Navarro Prieto, 2005).

Variable roles as behavioral concepts.

A role characterizes a variable through its successive values and how they are obtained (Sajaniemi, 2002; Sajaniemi and Navarro Prieto, 2005): a stepper follows a predictable progression, a gatherer combines contributions, and a most-wanted holder retains the best candidate encountered. Figure 2 summarizes all eleven Sajaniemi variable roles; Appendix M illustrates alternative implementations. Roles describe variable behavior, so role preservation differs from program equivalence: minimum and maximum computations can share a role, whereas equivalent programs can use variables with different roles. Although defined independently of the models, these roles can correlate with identifiers or syntax; testing their representation therefore requires controls for such surface cues.

Variable roles in neural models of code.

Hussain et al. (2023) detect steppers and walkers and inject their roles into Code2Seq representations. Demirtaş et al. (2025) use LLMs to detect programming plans in student programs. These studies use programming abstractions as input features or prediction targets; we compare role recoverability under controlled source edits with intervention outcomes during generation. This comparison requires annotations defined independently of model activations and linked to individual variables in natural code.

3 Annotating Variable Roles at Scale

To evaluate all eleven roles in multilingual natural code, we develop an automatic annotation procedure with explicit behavioral contracts.

Automatic role extraction.

Scaling annotation requires operational definitions of these cognitive abstractions. Prior systems cover subsets of the taxonomy, use execution traces, or adopt alternative definitions (Table 1). We operationalize all eleven Sajaniemi variable roles as explicit role contracts over Joern Code Property Graphs (CPGs), which represent syntax, control flow, and data dependencies (Yamaguchi et al., 2014). Queries recover initializations, updates, and uses, whose relationships are checked against the contracts. For example, the most-wanted holder contract links a candidate comparison to conditional replacement of the current value, with consistency checks on initialization and other writes. These static checks require neither execution nor a buildable project, enabling annotation of isolated source files. Appendix C gives the contracts and pseudocode.

Constructing a multilingual natural-code dataset.

We apply these contracts to CodeParrot GitHub-Code, combining an expanded annotation run with an earlier role-enriched subset, including Ruby. Deduplicating sources and matching declarations yields 126,926 files across five languages and 3,525,530 variables, of which 1,737,758 have at least one extracted role. Variables lacking a target annotation serve as candidate negatives, including any role instances missed by the extractor. For evaluation, we form five approximately equal folds stratified by role and language, keeping exact-source and detected clone groups intact. Appendix E reports role and language distributions.

Annotation validity and evaluation scope.

Source inspection and implementation checks informed contract refinement, but coverage remains limited to supported static patterns. A human evaluation on 660 stratified variables (Appendix D) assesses annotation quality, although its sampling design does not support corpus-wide precision or recall estimates. Counterfactual evaluation additionally uses case-level LLM review of original behavior and proposed edits (Appendix I). We therefore distinguish annotation accuracy on the evaluated subset from automatic-label prediction and sensitivity to reviewed edits.

4 Do Language Models Represent Variable Roles?

We first measure recoverability of role annotations, then test sensitivity to role-changing edits and stability under role-preserving renaming.

Matched prediction and diagnostic readout.

To reduce surface differences, we pair each annotated positive with a variable lacking that annotation, matching language and declaration kind and favoring similar surface characteristics. The test set contains 4,238 balanced pairs across eleven roles in C, C++, JavaScript, and Python. Because assignment targets often precede their determining expressions, we read the state of a target reference inserted after the selected statement or loop/conditional header. Appendix I records selection, exclusions, and fitting; Appendix L illustrates the contrasts.

Four predictors separate feature restriction from reconstruction.

We evaluate Gemma 2 2B, Gemma 3 4B/12B, Llama 3.1 8B, and Qwen3.5 9B at four layers each. SAEs encode residual activations as sparse feature vectors and reconstruct them through a linear decoder (Huben et al., 2024; Gao et al., 2024). Ridge probes on residual activations, SAE reconstructions, and 64 SAE features separate reconstruction fidelity from restricted feature readout; a single-feature predictor tests individual coordinates. Training fixes standardization, feature ranking, and polarity; validation selects regularization, the single feature, and decision thresholds. The name and code surface baselines are TF–IDF logistic classifiers over character nn-grams of the target name and the code prefix through the diagnostic token, respectively. Fits are frozen before evaluation; Appendix G lists SAE releases.

Matched recoverability exceeds the tested lexical baselines.

Residual probes exceed both surface baselines and individual SAE features in every role–model comparison (Figure 3). Averaging roles, models, and layers equally, average precision (AP) is 0.900.90 for residual probes and 0.720.72 for single features; constant-score AP is 0.500.50. Code features are competitive with individual SAE features: for most-wanted holder, their AP is 0.900.90, versus 0.750.75 for single features and 0.950.95 for residual probes. Reconstruction and top-64 probes close much of the single-feature gap (Table 2), showing the cost of restricting the readout to one coordinate.

Counterfactual ranking and classification give different answers.

To test whether matched recoverability tracks defining behavior, we evaluate edits that remove the target role. On 1,698 LLM-reviewed pairs from 948 source groups, residual probes rank originals above edited negatives with paired accuracy 0.8130.813–0.8770.877; ties receive half credit. The code-prefix baseline reaches 0.7500.750, while unchanged names give the name baseline 0.5000.500. Reconstruction probes fall 4.0–12.3 percentage points below residual probes, with all five paired 95% source-group bootstrap intervals excluding zero: reconstruction retains less counterfactual sensitivity. At the validation thresholds, however, residual probes classify 68–71% of edited negatives as positive, yielding balanced accuracy of 0.610–0.637. The scores therefore respond to role-changing edits more reliably than their binary decisions reject the edited examples.

Neutral target renaming preserves most ranking performance.

As a complementary role-preserving control, renaming both members of 100 test pairs per role reduces residual AUROC (area under the ROC curve) by 0.6–1.7 percentage points, to 0.878–0.887. On these same pairs, code-surface AUROC changes from 0.740 to 0.723 and name-surface AUROC from 0.602 to 0.492. Renaming preserves other identifiers, comments, and implementation cues, isolating sensitivity to the target spelling. Appendix H reports uncertainty and decision changes; Appendix J evaluates prompted recognition.

Readout and implementation condition the signal.

The diagnostic readout also matters because it follows the selected operation. At the second prescribed layer, residual counterfactual paired accuracy is 0.495–0.594 at the native identifier, 0.790–0.915 at statement end, and 0.856–0.920 at the inserted identifier. Separately fitted readouts thus expose much of this sensitivity at later unmodified positions. Even at the diagnostic readout, recoverability varies: with multilingual training, stepper AUROC ranges from 0.682 in JavaScript to 0.972 in Python; implementation contrasts can also be confounded by language (Appendix H).

Figure 4 illustrates the broader extrema, Boolean, and indexing associations of selected features. These contexts aid interpretation but do not establish role specificity (Appendix O). Neither contextual associations nor counterfactual sensitivity establish control; we next test interventions during generation.

5 Do Variable Role Representations Influence Code Generation?

To test control beyond recoverability, we apply activation addition and direction removal (Turner et al., 2023; Arditi et al., 2024; Ferrando et al., 2024; Tahimic and Cheng, 2025) on Mostly Basic Programming Problems (MBPP) (Austin et al., 2021). The SAE-feature experiments cover Gemma 2 2B and Gemma 3 4B/12B; a separate comparison normalizes probe and SAE directions under a correctness constraint. For each role rr, binary extractor labels on reference (RrefR_{\mathrm{ref}}) and unsteered (R0R_{0}) solutions define cohorts. These labels describe implementations: a correct alternative may use a different role. Target and random directions share eligible tasks; Pass@1 measures the fraction passing the supplied tests.

Reference-conditioned induction.

For feature ff, we add α​df\alpha d_{f}, where df=Wdec[f,:]d_{f}=W_{\mathrm{dec}}[f,:], to the residual stream at every generated token; RαR_{\alpha} denotes the resulting role annotation. The operational score sufficiency measures induction of an annotation present in the reference but absent from the baseline:

Sufficiencyr=P⁡(Rα⋆=1∣Rref=1,R0=0).\mathrm{Sufficiency}_{r}=P(R_{\alpha^{\star}}=1\mid R_{\mathrm{ref}}=1,R_{0}=0).

Eligible examples are split equally into calibration and test sets; α⋆\alpha^{\star} maximizes calibration sufficiency over a predefined strength grid and is fixed for testing. Reference-negative induction, denoted spurious induction in Figure 6, uses a separate cohort:

SpuriousInductionr=P⁡(Rα⋆=1∣Rref=0,R0=0).\mathrm{SpuriousInduction}_{r}=P(R_{\alpha^{\star}}=1\mid R_{\mathrm{ref}}=0,R_{0}=0).

Because reference-negative induction may yield a valid alternative, both cohorts require separate correctness evaluation.

Reference-conditioned suppression.

To test suppression of roles present in both reference and baseline, we normalize the decoder direction to d^f\hat{d}_{f} and orthogonalize matrices writing to the residual stream (Arditi et al., 2024; Ferrando et al., 2024; Tahimic and Cheng, 2025):

Wout′=Wout−(Wout​d^f⊤)​d^f.W_{\mathrm{out}}^{\prime}=W_{\mathrm{out}}-(W_{\mathrm{out}}\hat{d}_{f}^{\top})\hat{d}_{f}.

The operational score necessity is the frequency of role absence after removal, denoted by Rort=0R_{\mathrm{ort}}=0:

Necessityr=P⁡(Rort=0∣Rref=1,R0=1).\mathrm{Necessity}_{r}=P(R_{\mathrm{ort}}=0\mid R_{\mathrm{ref}}=1,R_{0}=1).

With no fitted strength, removal uses all eligible examples. Unlike generation-time addition, global removal also changes prompt processing; effect sizes reflect different perturbation scopes.

Removal suggests causal involvement with limited specificity.

Some Gemma 2 2B features have high necessity (Figure 6). Gatherer suppression exceeds its random-control range, whereas most-wanted holder’s score of 1.001.00 ties its control maximum. Their Pass@1 losses (−0.33-0.33 and −0.29-0.29) suggest suppression may partly reflect broader generation disruption, limiting evidence of role-specific control.

This correctness cost persists across all selected SAE features: removal suppresses annotations in 41/91, 72/109, and 131/187 target–task outcomes for Gemma 2 2B, Gemma 3 4B, and Gemma 3 12B. Only 2/91, 4/109, and 15/187 outcomes also pass the supplied tests; requiring both baseline and intervention to pass leaves 0, 3, and 13. Rates of annotation changes with passing tests exceed matched random controls by 1.3–3.7 percentage points for removal and 0.9–1.9 for addition, but all six task-grouped bootstrap 95% intervals include zero (Appendix Q). These joint outcomes show no clear advantage over random controls.

Weak sufficiency, partial structural effects.

Positive steering yields nonzero sufficiency scores of only 0.100.10–0.190.19, even where they exceed random-control ranges (Figure 6); low reference-negative induction likewise reflects weak effects. Yet Table 3 shows increased stepper-associated range calls under positive steering in both models, with smaller increases in gatherer-associated augmented assignments. These partial structural effects do not establish full-role sufficiency; other shifts are mixed. Only pairs with two clean parses contribute; Gemma 3 4B removal retains just 4/30 gatherer and 11/48 stepper pairs, from two and five tasks, limiting generalization.

Correctness-constrained calibration usually selects zero.

To test whether calibration can avoid these correctness costs, we constrain correctness in a normalized probe/SAE comparison; ten of eleven completed model–role cells select no intervention (Appendix N). In the remaining cell, each target direction produces one induction accompanied by passing tests among five eligible tasks, matching the random residual direction. Figure 5 illustrates repairs and failures, with selected successes and unfiltered random cases documented in Appendix P.

6 Related work

These distinctions connect work on behavior, representations, and interventions (Appendix K).

Behavioral robustness and semantic priors.

Semantics-preserving transformations test reliance on surface cues. ReCode finds reduced generation robustness after changes to identifiers, syntax, formatting, and docstrings (Wang et al., 2023); related mutations destabilize program-output predictions (Orvalho and Kwiatkowska, 2025). Masked-code models retain predictive ability after operand and branch reordering and identifier renaming, suggesting semantic learning (Ahmed et al., 2023).

Representations of programming concepts.

Probes recover syntax and structure (Karmakar and Robbes, 2021; Wan et al., 2022), including complete abstract syntax trees (Hernández López et al., 2022), and intermediate execution states in synthetic-language models (Jin and Rinard, 2024). Whereas probes target predefined properties, CoCoA discovers token-representation clusters and interprets their lexical, syntactic, and semantic content through static analysis and LLM annotation (Sharma et al., 2025). Variable roles let us compare residual and SAE recoverability under source edits, separating association from sensitivity to defining behavior.

Shared representations across programming and natural languages.

Cross-language studies test dependence on language-specific syntax. The same attention heads convey variable-type information across three programming languages (North et al., 2025), while language-specific and language-agnostic neurons coexist within a model (Yin et al., 2026). Intermediate-layer decoding and neuron ablations also reveal overlap with English (Kargaran et al., 2025). Our multilingual fits complement transfer studies by measuring variation in role recovery within each evaluated language.

Causal and mechanistic analyses.

Coding failures can coexist with useful computations: steering restores disrupted type predictions (Lucchetti and Guha, 2025), while synthetic parentheses analyses trace errors to interference between reliable and unreliable components (Rai et al., 2025). Yet SAE features predictive of code correctness need not support effective steering (Tahimic and Cheng, 2025). We extend this distinction to role annotations, comparing changes, joint passing outcomes, and matched random controls.

7 Conclusion, Limitations, and Future Work

Residual probes recover operational role annotations beyond tested lexical baselines. Combining SAE features narrows the single-feature gap, but reconstruction probes retain less sensitivity to reviewed role-changing edits. Removal suggests causal involvement with limited specificity and correctness costs, while positive steering yields weak full-role induction despite structural shifts.

Limitations.

Human evaluation shows that annotation quality varies substantially across roles, particularly for most-recent holder (Appendix D). These estimates come from a stratified sample and do not establish corpus-wide precision or recall; inter-annotator reliability also remains unmeasured. Decoding covers four layers per model and one source-group split, with uncertainty conditional on fitted predictors. The corpus includes development data without repository-level holdout, and target renaming retains other lexical cues. Interventions use small overlapping cohorts and finite prompt-visible tests, with unresolved historical scale provenance (Appendix Q).

Future work.

Our corpus combines natural-code complexity with independently defined roles and controlled source edits, offering a semi-controlled setting for studying conceptual abstraction beyond toy tasks. Future work can test whether role representations transfer to unseen languages and implementations, combine into higher-level programming plans, and support interventions that change variable behavior while preserving correctness.

8 Use of AI Assistance

We used large language models and coding agents to assist literature searches, manuscript drafting and revision, visualization code, and experimental protocols. The authors reviewed all references, procedures, figures, and manuscript content before inclusion. LLM reviewers also assessed counterfactual source edits, recording original-role validity, edited behavior, and rejection reasons; Appendix I distinguishes this procedure from human annotation validation.

AI assistance was more extensive in implementing the variable-role extractor, whose multilingual static-analysis rules combine syntax, control flow, and data flow. The authors specified behavioral requirements and rejection conditions for each role (Appendix C); coding agents implemented these contracts using Joern CPG facts and the existing extraction infrastructure. We inspected implementations and annotations manually on source-code examples and automatically through checks on annotations and intermediate variable facts. Failures and false positives or negatives informed contract refinements, followed by implementation updates and re-evaluation until both stabilized. The authors controlled the choice of taxonomy, operational definitions, final annotation rules, experimental design, interpretation, and manuscript.

Appendix contents

Appendix A Variable roles in real-world code

The simple examples in Figure 2 isolate each role’s behavior. The six excerpts below cover all eleven Sajaniemi variable roles in natural code from our annotated corpus. Common leading indentation is removed; long lines wrap for display.

Streaming an application release. Nextcloud App Store

The fixed value max_size bounds the download. The gatherer size adds input-dependent chunk lengths, and the one-way flag finished changes to true only after streaming completes. The temporary msg holds an exception message. The finally block uses the flag to clean up after an error.

Applying byte-level delta operations. Subvertpy

The walker action takes the operation code from each tuple in ops. The stepper i advances through the range of each target-copy operation. The container tview grows through bulk extension and single-byte appends. These roles coexist in a dispatch loop for different copy operations.

Reading blocks and emitting delta windows. Subvertpy

The most-recent holder text is replaced by each block read from the stream. Each block updates the digest and enters a delta window before the next read. A type check and a final callback surround this acquisition–use cycle.

Monitoring peak memory usage. ipython_memory_usage

The most-wanted holder peak_memory_usage retains the largest observed usage during each sampling run. Its monitoring loop also handles a stop signal, a sampling delay, and a timeout.

Searching parent directories for configuration. Projeny

The follower lastParentDir preserves parentDir’s old value before the next parent-directory step. Their comparison detects when traversal stops progressing; a file-existence check allows early return.

Computing a median with fallback handling. LIBXSMM

The organizer list_of_numbers sorts the elements; subsequent computation only reads the reordered list. The function also handles even-sized input, a fallback value, and empty input.

Appendix B Corpus sizes in prior variable-role studies

Table 4 expands Table 1, distinguishing source-code pools from labeled examples in each study’s reported units.

Comparability.

Programs, methods, and files are different source units, as are trace cases, declarations, and variable–role memberships. Counts do not imply matched deduplication, independent examples, or comparable holdouts. Role inventories and recognition rules also differ: Gerdt and Sajaniemi (2006) include Transformation but have no Temporary evaluation examples. Automatic annotations and downstream task performance do not establish role-label accuracy.

Coverage.

Our eleven-role, five-language corpus has more role-annotated variables than Hussain et al. (2023), but fewer steppers and walkers (Table 4). Coverage is uneven: Fixed Value accounts for 74.4% of role memberships, and Ruby for 53 files. Broader coverage does not imply more examples of each role or higher annotation quality.

Appendix C Variable-role extraction details

Section 8 describes how coding agents assisted implementation of these author-defined contracts.

Extraction pseudocode 1/3

vv: declaration identity; WW: binding writes; II: initialization events; U=W∖IU=W\setminus I; MM: observed state mutations; FF: raw Fixed Values. Initialization partitions are role-specific; named checks require supporting source/CPG evidence. CFG witnesses are bounded; missing labels do not prove semantic absence.

Supplement: src/role_extractor/scala/: facts/ builds evidence, role_predicates.sc classifies, annotation_emission.sc resolves labels. Frontend details and exact algorithms reside in this executable specification.

Fixed Value

1 if Q⁡(v)Q(v): return C⁡(v)=𝖥𝗂𝗑𝖾𝖽C(v)=\mathsf{Fixed}
2 require J⁡(v)J(v) and B⁡(v)B(v)
3 reject if any write violates AA, or Z⁡(v)Z(v) or O⁡(v)O(v) fails
4 accept

Key: QQ: verified non-text collection; CC: collection decision (third page). JJ: verified initialization, at most one per path (parameter entry; local initializer/exhaustive alternatives; member constructors). BB: no later/external rebinding. AA: plain, non-self-dependent writes. ZZ: no observed mutation. OO: no loop initialization/rebinding.

Pattern: limit = input_limit; use(limit)

Temporary (raw)

1 require L⁡(v)L(v), KT​(v)K_{T}(v), W≠∅W\neq\varnothing
2 for each w∈Ww\in W: require D⁡(w)D(w) and 1≤|Rw|≤51\leq|R_{w}|\leq 5
3 for each require 0≤d⁡(w,r)≤50\leq d(w,r)\leq 5 for every r∈Rwr\in R_{w}
4 return H⁡(v)H(v)

Key: LL: genuine callable-local; KTK_{T}: complete read associations. DD: direct plain non-self assignment; RHS call/known-variable token, excluding strings/keywords and import/definition artifacts. RwR_{w}: reaching-definition reads with redefinition-free CFG paths. dd: line difference; same-line event order; otherwise CFG instruction distance. HH: removing writes disconnects loop-entry/back-edge paths to reads.

Pattern: tmp = parse(item); emit(tmp)

One-Way Flag

1 b←b\leftarrow initial Boolean value; require Jb​(v)J_{b}(v), U≠∅U\neq\varnothing, M=∅M=\varnothing
2 for each w∈Uw\in U: require Tb​(w)T_{b}(w)
3 return some w∈Uw\in U satisfies Nb​(w)N_{b}(w)

Key: JbJ_{b}: complete canonical identity/partition, Boolean-literal initialization bb (also 0/1). TbT_{b}: complete direct write of ¬b\neg b, or v∨ev\lor e from false / v∧ev\land e from true; symmetric operands allowed. ee: Boolean literal/reference/comparison or supported logical composition. NbN_{b}: terminal assignment or non-inert operand; structural compatibility, not guard satisfiability.

Pattern: found = false; ...; found = found || match

Stepper

1 S←NS\leftarrow N
2 repeat S←S∪{v:P(v),Dv⊆F∪S,G(v,F,S)}S\leftarrow S\cup\{v:P(v),\ D_{v}\subseteq F\cup S,\ G(v,F,S)\}
3 until SS stops changing; return v∈Sv\in S

Key: NN: implicit numeric iterators. PP: complete repeated progression; every later write a direct self-update with unary +/−+/- or binary +,−,×,/+,-,\times,/; exclude fixed−v\text{fixed}-v and proved Walkers. DvD_{v}: non-self update dependencies. G⁡(v,F,S)G(v,F,S): complete supported guards; dependencies in SS or fixed inputs with predictable seeds (parameters allowed).

Pattern: i = 0; while i < limit: i += stride

Extraction pseudocode 2/3

Walker

1 if E⁡(v)E(v): accept
2 require KW​(v)K_{W}(v) and U≠∅U\neq\varnothing
3 for each w∈Uw\in U: require V⁡(w)V(w)
4 accept

Key: EE: implicit element iterator, excluding numeric iterators. KWK_{W}: complete navigation and initialization partition. VV: previous-position dependence; loop context; access/control use; resolved member, fixed-collection successor index, supported navigation call, or cursor increment/decrement with direct cursor use. An ordinary array index alone is insufficient.

Pattern: while p: use(p); p = p.next

Most Recent Holder

1 require KR​(v)K_{R}(v) and Av≠∅A_{v}\neq\varnothing
2 reject if Walker, Follower, or Most Wanted Holder
3 if member: return PR​(v)P_{R}(v)
4 return LR​(v)L_{R}(v) and every a∈Ava\in A_{v} has witness R⁡(a)R(a)

Key: KRK_{R}: complete acquisition/correction coverage of UU, M=∅M=\varnothing, no holder-dependent acquisition guard. AvA_{v}: acquisitions (call, collection access, iterator projection). LRL_{R}: non-member loop/proved-iterator context. RR: read outside own writes via one unambiguous stable-input correction chain; limits: depth 64, nodes 10,000, corrections 5, branches 128. PRP_{R}: same-owner member acquisitions in ordinary methods plus an owner use; no cross-call ordering proof.

Pattern: while more: current = read(); consume(current)

Follower

1 require KF​(v)K_{F}(v); reject if X⁡(v)X(v)
2 s←s\leftarrow unique master shared by every non-initial assignment
3 require As​(w)A_{s}(w) for every reassignment ww
4 return Ys​(v)Y_{s}(v)

Key: KFK_{F}: complete, nonempty reassignment set UFU_{F}. AsA_{s}: uniquely resolved canonical declaration/member/fixed-index master; RHS ss, s+ks+k, k+sk+s, or s−ks-k; kk literal/raw Fixed Value. YsY_{s}: every local loop has capture →\to master evolution →\to follower use →\to capture; members require ordered capture/evolution per writing method and same-owner use. XX: self-dependence, mutation, follower-controlled write, or follower-dependent master evolution.

Pattern: prev = current; current = next(current); use(prev)

Most Wanted Holder

1 𝖯𝗋𝗂𝗆𝖺𝗋𝗒​(v)←JS​(v)\mathsf{Primary}(v)\leftarrow J_{S}(v) and S⁡(v)S(v) and KS​(v)K_{S}(v)
2 clear primary status if Stepper, Walker, Gatherer, or Follower
3 accept if 𝖯𝗋𝗂𝗆𝖺𝗋𝗒⁡(v)\mathsf{Primary}(v)
4 otherwise accept if some primary hh satisfies Bh​(v)B_{h}(v)

Key: JSJ_{S}: compatible seeds, nonempty loop-selection epochs, one direction. SS: guarded holder–candidate comparison, min/max, or null-seeded first-satisfying candidate with structural exit. KSK_{S}: all writes explained (seed/selection/unset fallback), no mutation. BhB_{h}: nonempty later writes all coupled to one primary hh by a unique guard in one context; nonempty fixed/stepper/walker dependencies, later read, no mutation.

Pattern: if score > best: best = score; winner = i

Extraction pseudocode 3/3

Gatherer

1 require KG​(v)K_{G}(v), JG​(v)J_{G}(v), 𝒜v≠∅\mathcal{A}_{v}\neq\varnothing
2 reject if Stepper or Walker
3 for each span a∈𝒜va\in\mathcal{A}_{v}: require a self-update with DD
4 require all resets, other transforms, and finalizations satisfy TT
5 accept

Key: KGK_{G}: admitted numeric non-collection; complete phase coverage of UU. JGJ_{G}: parameter, stable numeric seed, or supported first contribution. 𝒜\mathcal{A}: nonempty loop spans split by resets. 𝖲𝖾𝗅𝖿𝖴𝗉𝖽𝖺𝗍𝖾\mathsf{SelfUpdate}: uses the previous value. DD: indexed/member/dereferenced data or a non-fixed/non-stepper dependency; calls through argument data. TT: numeric/fixed resets; arithmetic transforms with numeric/fixed/stepper inputs; at most one stable arithmetic finalization per method outside loops.

Pattern: score *= 5; score += points[item]

Container

1 require Q⁡(v)Q(v) and Hc​(v)H_{c}(v)
2 Ec←E_{c}\leftarrow post-construction collection changes
3 Pc←P_{c}\leftarrow event IDs consumed by proved permutation spans Π\Pi
4 return Ec∖Pc≠∅E_{c}\setminus P_{c}\neq\varnothing

Key: QQ: verified non-text collection; HcH_{c}: source-backed target, excluding synthetic/function bindings. EcE_{c}: changes after the identified construction phase: rebinding, updates, add/remove/clear, element/descendant writes, exact-target mutations. Π\Pi: proved permutations; PcP_{c}: event IDs they consume. Alias-only effects do not establish mutation.

Pattern: items.append(x); items.sort()

Organizer

1 require Q⁡(v)Q(v), Hc​(v)H_{c}(v), and Jc​(v)J_{c}(v)
2 require Πv≠∅\Pi_{v}\neq\varnothing
3 return Ec∖Pc=∅E_{c}\setminus P_{c}=\varnothing

Key: JcJ_{c}: verified, complete collection initialization. Π\Pi: tuple swap; local dataflow swap; exact same-collection swap; known in-place sort/reverse/shuffle/rotate. Manual swaps require reaching-definition/CFG witnesses without transformation; ambiguous paths, indexes, or aliases fail. KcK_{c}: complete collection lifecycle.

Pattern: items.reverse()

Collection decision and final labels

1 C⁡(v)←𝖭𝗈𝗇𝖾C(v)\leftarrow\mathsf{None}; require Q⁡(v)Q(v) and Hc​(v)H_{c}(v)
2 if Ec∖Pc≠∅E_{c}\setminus P_{c}\neq\varnothing: C⁡(v)←𝖢𝗈𝗇𝗍𝖺𝗂𝗇𝖾𝗋C(v)\leftarrow\mathsf{Container}
3 else if Jc​(v)J_{c}(v) and Πv≠∅\Pi_{v}\neq\varnothing: C⁡(v)←𝖮𝗋𝗀𝖺𝗇𝗂𝗓𝖾𝗋C(v)\leftarrow\mathsf{Organizer}
4 else if Jc​(v)J_{c}(v) and Kc​(v)K_{c}(v): C⁡(v)←𝖥𝗂𝗑𝖾𝖽C(v)\leftarrow\mathsf{Fixed}

Emission: retain raw multilabel results subject to exclusions above. Suppress Temporary if any role other than Fixed Value co-occurs; otherwise Temporary suppresses Fixed Value. Member subjects omit Temporary, Gatherer, and Most Wanted Holder. Raw Fixed Values remain available to dependency checks. Emit identity, labels, metadata, and exact source views; graph/alias/interprocedural limits follow the supplementary implementation.

Appendix D Variable Role Extractor Human Evaluation

Annotation protocol.

Because Sajaniemi’s roles describe cognitive rather than strictly syntactic properties of variables, we assess the extractor against human annotations. Given the size of the corpus and the highly uneven role distribution, we construct a stratified sample combining extractor positives with two types of negatives.

For each of the 11 roles, we sample 20 variables assigned that role by the extractor and 20 variables not assigned that role but whose names suggest it (e.g., best for most-wanted holder). Rather than defining these semantic priors manually, we identify identifier substrings that best discriminate each role in the extracted corpus, ranked by their F1 score, and use them to sample potential false negatives. This enriches the sample with plausible missed instances of rare roles, such as follower, which would be unlikely to appear in a random sample and would otherwise make recall difficult to assess. We additionally sample 220 variables without any extracted role, yielding 660 distinct variables.

Variables are presented in random order, with their identifier occurrences highlighted in a code excerpt containing all variable occurrences. The annotator assigns one of the 11 roles or “no role”, without access to extractor predictions or sampling strata.

Evaluation.

We treat human annotations as reference labels and evaluate the extractor as a multi-label classifier, reporting one-vs-rest precision, recall, and F1 for each role. Table 5 summarizes the sample and human-label distributions, and reports the resulting scores. Because the sample deliberately balances roles and enriches negatives with semantic priors, these unweighted scores characterize the selected subset rather than corpus-wide performance.

Appendix E Dataset statistics

The consolidated corpus combines the earlier role-enriched dataset with variable records from successful shards of the expanded CodeParrot annotation run. Of 150,000 new candidate files, thirteen shards completed and two failed parsing; failed shards contribute no new annotations. We merge byte-identical sources and identify variables by source hash, kind, name, and declaration coordinates, preserving both releases’ annotation IDs. The corpus contains 126,926 source files, 14,624,580 physical lines, and 3,525,530 unique variables across five languages, retaining the earlier Ruby data. Of these, 1,737,758 have an extracted role and 1,787,772 have none; missing labels do not imply semantic absence of a role.

Five approximately equal file folds are stratified by role and language with source groups kept intact. For the baselines, three folds train, one validates, and one tests, yielding 2,116,300/705,213/704,017 variables (Table 6). The corpus includes 2,428,645 locals, 865,797 parameters, and 231,088 members.

Fixed value contributes 74.4% of the 1,747,627 memberships, while follower and organizer have 724 and 747 variables (Table 7). There are 9,866 multi-role variables; the largest overlap is fixed value with walker, for 5,665 variables.

Integrity and scope.

Exact-source matches, normalized whole-file/function matches, and earlier clone links define 122,458 indivisible source groups; none crosses folds. This grouping is not repository holdout or exhaustive semantic deduplication; 16,784 files have parser errors. We union existential boolean flags across duplicates and recover flags for variables with no extracted role from raw facts. The earlier corpus was used in model development; the new split does not erase that exposure.

Appendix F Metadata and lexical baselines

We use the full consolidated corpus (Appendix E), without subsampling. The split has 2,116,300 training, 705,213 validation, and 704,017 test variables. For each of eleven roles, variables lacking that annotation, including those with no extracted role, are negative. We evaluate extractor labels using original identifiers.

Predictors and selection.

We use language/kind categories, six general boolean properties, and TF–IDF name character 1–4-grams or local-code token/operator 1–2-grams. Vocabularies retain at most 12,000 name and 30,000 code features, with minimum document frequency 3. Code windows cover up to eight occurrences with 100 source bytes per side; verified target identifiers are masked. The combined baseline concatenates name, code, and boolean features; role-specific metadata and target-derived flags are excluded. For each role, class-balanced L2 logistic regression selects C∈{0.1,1,10}C\in\{0.1,1,10\} by validation AP and a threshold by validation F1. Vocabularies and weights are refitted on 2,821,513 train/validation variables; thresholds are unchanged.

Train/validation frequencies define binary majority (no roles) and most-frequent-role (fixed value) references; always positive predicts every role. Uniform random scores yield positive predictions with probability 0.50.5 or the train/validation role frequency. AP integrates precision over recall increments at distinct score thresholds; F1 is 2​TP/(2​TP+FP+FN)2\mathrm{TP}/(2\mathrm{TP}+\mathrm{FP}+\mathrm{FN}) at the frozen threshold. Constant-score AP equals test prevalence; macro averages weight roles equally.

Binary majority attains 95.5% accuracy with zero F1. Name, code, and combined macro AP are 0.142, 0.487, and 0.533 (Tables 8–9). These scores measure automatic-label predictability, without independent semantic validation. Probe comparisons require matched subjects, negatives, partitions, and accessible context; these windows can include code after a causal readout.

Appendix G SAE Details

Appendix H Additional Analyses of Role Representations

On matched pairs, residual probes recover automatic labels more accurately than individual SAE features, and surface cues also predict these labels. We next test how this discrimination changes with target names, language, implementation, and the observation position. These analyses use the fitted predictors and diagnostic readout from Section 4, averaging four layers except in the readout comparison. The principal comparisons use matched-negative training; the broader sweep trains separately on matched, neighboring-role, same-context, and hard-mined negatives and evaluates all six strategies in Appendix L. For thresholded results, validation fixes each decision threshold by maximizing sensitivity minus false-positive rate. We use Gemma Scope for Gemma 2 2B (Lieberum et al., 2024), Gemma Scope 2 for Gemma 3 4B and 12B (McDougall et al., 2025), Llama Scope for Llama 3.1 8B (He et al., 2024), and Qwen-Scope for Qwen3.5 9B (Deng et al., 2026).

Reconstruction and counterfactual controls.

To separate reconstruction loss from the restriction to one feature, we also fit ridge probes to SAE reconstructions and to the 64 training-ranked features. Across models, their matched-negative macro AUROC reaches 0.857–0.881 and 0.853–0.878, respectively, compared with 0.906–0.913 for residual probes (Table 2). Thus, combining features closes much of the single-feature gap. We also test 1,698 source-reviewed role-changing counterfactual pairs from 948 source groups, excluding rejected edits and incorrect original-role labels through the LLM review described in Appendix I. Paired accuracy measures how often an original ranks above its edited negative, assigning ties half credit. Residual paired accuracy is 0.813–0.877; reconstruction probes are 4.0–12.3 percentage points lower, with all five paired 95% intervals excluding zero. SAE reconstruction therefore reduces recoverability of these distinctions under the tested linear fits. Intervals use 1,000 source-group bootstrap draws, with equal role and layer weight, conditional on the fixed split and fits. At the same frozen validation thresholds, residual-probe false-positive rates on edited negatives are 0.684–0.713, with balanced accuracy 0.610–0.637. These decision metrics distinguish sensitivity of score rankings from successful rejection of edited negatives.

Target names contribute to discrimination.

To isolate target-name sensitivity, we select 100 Test pairs per role without consulting scores and replace every occurrence of the resolved target binding with a neutral identifier. Both positive and negative variables are renamed, preserving their roles and the surrounding syntax; fitted choices are unchanged. Both name conditions use the same model, SAE, and inference configuration. Residual AUROC decreases by 0.6–1.7 percentage points across models (Figure 8b), remaining at 0.878–0.887 after renaming. Single-feature AUROC is lower, at 0.693–0.760, with changes between −0.8-0.8 and +0.1+0.1 points. On these same intervention pairs, name surface features fall from AUROC 0.602 to 0.492, whereas code surface features change from 0.740 to 0.723. The residual probe preserves more discrimination than either surface baseline, although its frozen decisions still change for 10.8% of positives and 12.4% of negatives. Its balanced accuracy decreases from 0.830 to 0.809, distinguishing stable ranking from stable thresholded decisions. The edit preserves other identifiers, comments, and implementation cues, so it measures sensitivity to the target name.

Language and implementation condition the measured signal.

We supplement Test coverage toward 50 matched pairs per supported role/language and examine metadata-defined realizations (Figure 9). The fits retain their original multilingual training and validation populations, and evaluation covers C, C++, JavaScript and Python. Gatherer and one-way flag have high residual AUROC across all four languages, while stepper ranges from 0.682 in JavaScript to 0.972 in Python. Ranking and thresholded decisions also differ across implementations: single-feature stepper AUROC is similar for for-loop and other updates (0.728 versus 0.757), but recall drops from 0.895 to 0.624 at the validation thresholds. Within Python, its recall also falls from 0.904 to 0.750, on 23 and 30 positives respectively. Most-wanted-holder recall is high for both guarded replacement and min/max selection, especially for residual probes (0.994 and 0.966). Walker differences are entangled with language in the selected subtypes, and member-expression most-recent holders lack a supported diagnostic readout. These distinctions constrain which apparent subtype effects can be attributed to implementation.

The observation point determines which edits are visible.

Causal attention makes the readout position consequential: an assignment’s identifier can precede the expression that determines its role. At the second prescribed layer, residual paired accuracy on reviewed edits is 0.495–0.594 at the native identifier and 0.856–0.920 at the diagnostic identifier (Figure 8). Statement-end readouts recover much of this sensitivity, with residual paired accuracy of 0.790–0.915 on the unmodified input. These separately fitted readouts measure position-specific decodability: later positions expose source text that can be unavailable at the native identifier, and the diagnostic reference also changes the input. The resulting predictive associations motivate the intervention experiments in Section 5.

Appendix I Evaluation populations, review, and selection

The full annotation corpus, representation benchmark, and generation tasks answer different questions. Table 11 identifies their populations and selection units.

Frozen representation cohort.

The representation experiments retain an earlier prepared cohort and its source/clone-group assignments; the expanded corpus’s full-variable baselines are a separate evaluation. One rotation assigns folds 2/3/4 to training, fold 1 to validation, and fold 0 to Test. Training and validation retain their original multilingual populations. The original matched Test cohort contains 4,245 pairs; excluding Ruby pairs and the two source-role labels rejected by subsequent review leaves 4,238. The common tokenization support uses a 4,096-token ceiling. All methods and model–SAE systems share eligible pairs within a comparison; the four prescribed layers are averaged without Test-based layer selection.

Negative selection.

Matched negatives share the positive’s partition, programming language, and declaration kind, and lack the target annotation. Retrieval ranks candidates using standardized context length, occurrence count, name length and shape, counts of loops, branches, assignments and calls, parser status, and identifier spelling similarity. Scaling is fitted on training subjects; candidates from the positive’s source group are excluded, with limits on negative reuse. Neighboring-role selection additionally requires a specified competing role; same-context selection chooses another resolved binding in the enclosing context. Hard-negative selection uses a logistic classifier on target-masked code, fitted with source-group-held-out folds within training. The broader sweep varies the training-negative policy, retaining matched-negative validation; the main comparisons use matched training throughout.

Predictor fitting.

Residual, reconstruction, and top-64 probes use ridge regression with training-only centering and coordinate scaling. The coordinate standard-deviation floor is 10−610^{-6}, and standardized vectors are divided by the square root of their dimension. Validation AUROC selects the penalty from {10−6,10−4,10−2,1,100}\{10^{-6},10^{-4},10^{-2},1,100\}. Training AUROC ranks SAE coordinates by max⁡(AUROC,1−AUROC)\max(\mathrm{AUROC},1-\mathrm{AUROC}) and fixes their predictive polarity. Validation selects one of the top 64 coordinates for the single-feature predictor; the multi-feature probe uses those same 64 candidates. For each predictor, validation selects the threshold maximizing sensitivity minus false-positive rate. The matched name and visible-prefix baselines fit TF–IDF/logistic models on the same training pairs and use validation for regularization and threshold selection. Name features use character 2–5-grams and a 12,000-feature cap; code prefixes use 3–5-grams and a 30,000-feature cap. Both use minimum document frequency two, case-sensitive sublinear term frequencies, and validation-selected C∈{0.1,1,10}C\in\{0.1,1,10\}. The code-prefix input ends at the diagnostic identifier; the full-corpus lexical windows in Appendix F use a different context policy.

Counterfactual review and exclusions.

Counterfactuals are generated from eligible source patterns and reviewed through LLM assessments of the enclosing binding context and exact edit. Review records specify whether the original has the target role, whether the edit removes it, source-level validity, and assumptions about external inputs or calls. The rubric asks reviewers to inspect the binding lifetime and all writes, including mutation and aliasing, and to flag unresolved dependencies or role ambiguity. Source annotations and proposed edits are supplied as fallible evidence; the judgments are not blinded to those proposals. The final review uses GPT-5.6 Terra source reviewers to resolve 333 previously pending cases: 330 edits are accepted and three rejected. One rejected edit preserves the target role; two cases have incorrect original-role labels. Those two source-role labels are excluded from affected test panels; training and validation fits are unchanged. The resulting 1,698 accepted pairs include earlier reviewed cases and the final accepted additions after evaluation exclusions. These static LLM judgments are distinct from independent human adjudication or execution-based verification; the acceptance fraction of the selected queue is not an estimate of corpus-wide annotation accuracy. Review uncertainty and inter-annotator agreement are unmeasured.

Ranking, decisions, and uncertainty.

Paired counterfactual accuracy is 𝔼⁡[𝟏​(soriginal>sedit)+12​𝟏​(soriginal=sedit)]\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{1}(s_{\mathrm{original}}>s_{\mathrm{edit}})+\tfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{1}(s_{\mathrm{original}}=s_{\mathrm{edit}})]. AUROC instead compares all positive/negative score combinations within a role–layer cell. Balanced accuracy is the mean of positive recall and negative recall at the frozen threshold. Model summaries average roles and layers equally. Paired 95% intervals use 1,000 joint source-group bootstrap resamples, retaining related examples and methods together; they condition on the split, fits, and review decisions. Layer ranges in Figure 3 and random-feature ranges in Figure 6 describe heterogeneity, not sampling intervals.

Neutral names and readout controls.

Test-pair selection does not consult predictor scores. Neutral identifiers are derived from a role-independent binding hash; edits replace all annotated occurrences of the resolved binding, with source hashes, syntax shape, and non-target leaf bytes checked. Original and renamed comparisons use matched execution settings; stored scores are reused only after overlap checks. Readout controls fit separate predictors at the native identifier, statement end, and inserted identifier at each model’s second prescribed layer. They compare position-specific decodability, with differences in accessible context and, for the inserted reference, input text.

Steering selection and provenance.

The representative features in Figure 6 are a descriptive selection from the larger feature-scale experiment. The archived selection does not establish that these five representatives were chosen before intervention outcomes were inspected; aggregate conclusions therefore use all selected targets within each protocol. Addition strength is calibrated on annotation induction for the feature-scale experiments, while the normalized experiments calibrate a joint induction-and-passing objective subject to a correctness constraint. Appendices N and Q report their different perturbation scopes, task overlap, denominators, and unresolved historical scale provenance.

Appendix J Behavioral role recognition and prompt sensitivity

We evaluate Llama 3.2 1B/3B and 3.1 8B, Gemma 3 1B/4B/12B/27B, Qwen3 1.7B/4B/8B/14B Base, and Qwen3.5 9B Base. These twelve pretrained checkpoints share the protocol but vary in size, architecture, and training.

Evaluation and scoring.

The same 9,553 matched positive/negative development pairs cover eleven roles and five languages: 17,770 distinct role/variable queries from 16,837 variables and 6,996 source groups. Labels are automatic annotations; a negative lacks the target annotation. Prompts include the role definition, full enclosing code with comments, and target identifier and location, asking for a judgment from initialization, updates, and use while allowing other roles to apply. Each role has one fixed training-only demonstration set (seed 17), with nested, class-balanced prefixes of 0, 2, 4, or 8 examples shared across models. Inference uses BF16 without quantization, chat templates, or source truncation. At the final Answer: position, s=log⁡P⁡(Yes)−log⁡P⁡(No)s=\log P(\texttt{Yes})-\log P(\texttt{No}) predicts positive when s≥0s\geq 0; average precision (AP) ranks the unrounded scores. We restore original pair multiplicities and average roles equally: constant predictions attain 50% accuracy and constant scores attain 50% AP.

Recognition across checkpoints.

Gemma 3 27B has the highest eight-shot macro accuracy/AP (72.1/77.2%; Figure 10); its accuracy exceeds Gemma 3 12B by 5.8 points (paired 95% interval: 4.6–6.9). Qwen3 14B reaches 68.1/72.6%, exceeding Qwen3 8B accuracy by 8.7 points (7.5–9.9). Eight-shot accuracy rises with tested size within each family, but demonstration gains vary: the eight-minus-zero accuracy intervals include zero for Qwen3 1.7B/4B/8B, and their AP does not improve. Llama 3.2 1B gains 1.0 accuracy point (0.3–1.7), with accuracy near chance.

Taxonomy-free descriptions.

Prompts request at most three sentences on initialization, updates, and use, without role names or examples. Training-only format calibration reduces descriptions reaching the generation cap from 27/66 to 6/66 across three checkpoints; we fix this format for all models. Cap rates range from 0% to 78.2% across the expanded model set. We assess fidelity qualitatively: Gemma 3 27B invents a prior None initialization for exit_code, while Qwen3 14B identifies the shown assignment.

J.1 Role differences and free generation

Role and answer dependence.

Fixed value, most-recent holder, and temporary are weaker than one-way flag and most-wanted holder (Figure 11). Greedy generation evaluates 100 distinct development cases per role (50 positive, 50 negative), shared across models: 1,100 cases and 39,600 outputs across descriptions and zero/eight-shot answers. The fixed seeded panel includes the original six cases per role; cases receive equal weight and share source groups. Leading Yes/No answers are valid; invalid outputs count as incorrect, with a 512-new-token budget. Three Llama 3.1 8B shards use A100/GB10 GPUs; the others use H200s, with matching software.

Eight-shot answer validity is 97.6–100%, yet 95.5–100% of outputs reach the cap (Figure 12). Gemma 3 27B reaches 73.2% free-answer accuracy. Qwen3 Base checkpoints yield 99.8–100% valid zero-shot starts, compared with 6/1,100 for Qwen3.5 9B despite its 70.1% zero-shot AP under constrained scoring.

Appendix L Selecting and generating negative examples

Appendix M Different realizations of variable roles

Appendix N Matched probe and SAE steering

We compare probe and SAE directions under the same intervention budget, alongside random residual and random SAE directions. The exploratory panel covers stepper, gatherer, most-wanted holder, and walker in Gemma 2 2B (layer 13), Gemma 3 12B (layer 24), and Llama 3.1 8B (layer 16). Each role has twelve calibration tasks and twelve Test tasks, balanced by role presence in the reference solution and shared across models. These are intact batches selected from the original MBPP cohort without consulting generation outcomes. Eleven model–role cells pass the generation and evaluation checks; Llama walker is excluded because its zero-dose output differs from the unsteered baseline.

A common budget and calibration criterion.

We add each normalized direction at generated-token residual positions in one layer, with magnitudes of 1%, 3%, or 10% of the median calibration residual norm. The zero-strength option is also eligible. Probe and SAE share the strength maximizing mean calibration induction accompanied by passing tests, subject to each losing at most five percentage points of correctness; ties favor the smaller strength. The selected strength is fixed for Test and applied to both random controls. With twelve calibration tasks, the correctness constraint permits no net loss of a passing program. All conditions retain the same four-task batches, prompts, and greedy 256-token budget, and the zero-dose control must reproduce baseline tokens exactly. The completed comparison contains 3,696 evaluated generations.

Role induction often accompanies test failure.

Gemma 2 2B most-wanted holder selects the 10% dose (Figure 21). Its probe and SAE induction rates are 3/5 and 4/5, compared with 1/5 for the random residual direction and 0/5 for the random SAE direction. Induction accompanied by passing tests is 1/5 for the probe, SAE, and random residual direction, and 0/5 for the random SAE direction. Overall Test correctness remains 4/12 for both target directions and falls to 3/12 for both controls. The remaining ten cells select zero because nonzero strengths provide no better feasible calibration objective. This result distinguishes the ability to alter role annotations from reliable control under a correctness constraint. These estimates concern positive steering at one layer in small, overlapping task cohorts conditioned on baseline role presence.

Appendix O Activation contexts of role-associated SAE features

The displays below cover all eleven roles with validation-selected single-feature predictors from Gemma 3 4B layers 9 and 17. Role colors and symbols follow Figure 2. Each row gives a Neuronpedia description, corpus code (left and “Also”), and public prose (right). Highlight intensity is linear from zero to the displayed bound, fixed per latent; compare magnitudes within a latent. “Lower predicts role” identifies negative polarity in the original probe selection, so strong highlighting need not occur on the target variable.

All ten distinct latents were measured on 41 hand-selected training snippets. Code crops retain their standalone-input activations; public windows retain their original Neuronpedia contexts. These examples illustrate activity, not prevalence.

Descriptions and activation contexts (continued)

Matched and reviewed-counterfactual AUROCs are 0.848/0.474 for most-wanted holder, 0.949/0.354 for one-way flag, and 0.764/0.536 for stepper. Contextual activity alone does not establish role specificity.

Appendix P Qualitative outcomes of SAE steering

The larger Gemma 2 2B and Gemma 3 4B experiments from Section 5 also permit inspection of complete generated programs. Across 292 evaluated target–task pairs, eight failing-to-passing transitions correspond to six distinct model–task pairs. They include most-frequent-item search, counting sort, largest row sum, cuboid volume, product divided by length, and maximum subarray sum. We show selected repairs and failures alongside an unfiltered seeded random sample in Figure 5. All displayed test outcomes were reproduced on the complete programs using the three supplied assertions.

The selected repairs can reveal useful changes, such as replacing a stub with an explicit search, without establishing that the targeted role caused the improvement. In the broader gallery, cuboid and product repairs pass all three tests while retaining a zero target-role annotation. Conversely, an unchanged correct program may already implement the role semantically even when its original annotation is absent. The six random cases drawn across the full gallery all fail the supplied tests; the draw was not repeated to obtain favorable examples. These observations motivate reading role annotations, complete code, and correctness together.

Appendix Q Consolidated quantitative analysis of causal interventions

We connect the selected-feature results in Figure 6 and the structural changes in Table 3 to all tested SAE features and the normalized probe/SAE experiments. The two displays summarize complementary measurements from the same Gemma 2 2B and Gemma 3 4B causal runs. The analysis adds the completed Gemma 3 12B feature-scale run, a five-fit Gemma 3 12B stepper pilot, and the eleven model–role cells in Appendix N.

Across all historical features, removal changes 41/91, 72/109, and 131/187 target–task outcomes for Gemma 2 2B, Gemma 3 4B, and Gemma 3 12B, respectively. Only 2/91, 4/109, and 15/187 also pass the supplied tests; requiring both outputs to pass leaves 0, 3, and 13 outcomes. The joint outcome exceeds matched random controls by only 1.3, 1.4, and 3.7 percentage points for removal, and 1.9, 1.3, and 0.9 points for addition; all six corresponding intervals include zero. These enrollment counts include repeated tasks across features and are not independent sample sizes. The removal cohorts contain 32, 32, and 63 unique tasks, respectively; reference-positive addition uses 53, 49, and 45 unique Test tasks.

Q.1 Comparison units, calibration, and structural survival

Protocol-specific comparisons.

We test eleven SAE directions in Gemma 2 2B and Gemma 3 4B and nine in Gemma 3 12B, covering five roles. They share a union of 121 MBPP tasks with role-specific enrollment; removal uses both splits, while induction uses Test only. Six positive multipliers are calibrated for annotation induction, with ten same-layer random SAE controls per target. The baseline passing counts are 33/121, 14/121, and 67/121. The archived feature scales are not normalized across models, and twenty of the shared package’s twenty-two scales differ from the corresponding selection artifact’s training-positive maximum. They are treated as executed settings with unresolved scale provenance. Consequently, these results describe the recorded interventions without attributing cross-model differences to model size or a common dose.

The normalized stepper pilot uses Gemma 3 12B layer 31, five fitted probes, and the same SAE feature in every fit. It has 48 calibration and 144 Test tasks, including 43 eligible removal and 53 induction tasks. Four fits select zero and one selects a 1% residual-norm dose under the correctness constraint. In that nonzero fit, probe and SAE directions each induce stepper on 2/53 tasks; two probe outputs and one SAE output pass, including one probe change that preserves baseline correctness. Repeated SAE outcomes and overlapping probe training sets are not independent replications. Local projection affects one generated-token layer; global projection also alters residual writers and prompt processing. The smaller extension in Appendix N instead covers four roles in twelve-task splits and selects zero in ten of eleven completed cells.

Syntax and correctness condition different subsets.

For Gemma 3 4B removal, gatherer syntax uses 4/30 pairs from two distinct tasks, and stepper syntax uses 11/48 pairs from five tasks. The reported shifts therefore describe parseable survivors, not all interventions. Among the three clean stepper pairs where both outputs pass, the range-call frequency does not change.

Scope of inference.

Within each protocol, target and control outcomes use the same eligible tasks and retained denominator. The joint metric requires the intervention output to pass; preserving an already correct program additionally requires baseline correctness. Intervals condition on selected features, fitted probes, calibration, and sampled controls; all-zero samples can yield degenerate intervals. The evaluated records share twelve task IDs between historical runs and the smaller extension, four between the pilot and extension, and none between historical runs and the pilot. No effect is pooled across protocols. Finite, prompt-visible tests, generated-code truncation, and missing historical zero-dose/batch-parity audits limit claims of semantic control.
